title: What will my treatment cost? estimator
seen: 16 of 22 HFEA reviewers said they paid "way above the estimate". The prices page is about 8,000px long on a phone with 34 accordions, and medication, freezing and add-ons are listed separately under each package.
idea: A short tool: pick a package, answer three or four questions (ICSI likely? freezing? medication top-ups?), and see a likely total, a range and the staged payments, with every assumption shown. Ends with 'Book a free information session to check this'.
payback: Price shock after the first consultation is the most expensive drop-out, because the clinic has already spent clinical time on that person. An honest total up front filters out people who can't afford it and keeps the ones who can. It should also move the HFEA 'did you pay what you expected' score, which every comparison shopper sees.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (personalised costed plan); Bourn Hall (fixed-price packages)

title: One source of truth for prices and criteria
seen: PURE criteria differ between the prices page (37 and under, AMH 6–35, BMI below 35) and the PURE page (under 38, AMH above 10, BMI below 30, regular periods). Prices are typed into each page and into two PDFs.
idea: Hold packages, prices, inclusions and criteria once, as Wagtail snippets, and pull them into the prices page, each package page, the estimator and the comparison table.
payback: Every contradiction costs a phone call and some trust. One place to update each April also saves editor time and removes the risk of quoting the wrong price.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (one itemised price list, criteria up front)

title: Package comparison table
seen: First, PURE, PURE Duo, Plus, Plus Duo and Multi-Cycle are each explained on separate pages and in separate accordions, so the difference between them is hard to see.
idea: One side-by-side table: who it's for, criteria, what's included, price, price per cycle and how payments are staged. Highlight that Duo and Multi are paid in stages.
payback: Multi-Cycle (£11,540) and the Duo packages are worth more than a single PURE cycle (£5,240) and give patients a better cumulative chance. Showing the per-cycle saving and staged payments side by side is the clearest upsell the site can make, and it's an honest one.
at: Bourn Hall (multi-cycle with savings shown); CARE (pricing page)

title: Which package am I likely to be eligible for?
seen: Eligibility for First, PURE, Plus and Multi-Cycle depends on age, AMH, BMI and previous cycles, but people have to read four pages to work it out (and get two answers for PURE).
idea: Four questions (age, AMH if known, BMI, previous IVF) that point to the likely package and price, with a BMI helper and a clear 'your consultant will confirm this'.
payback: Gets people to the right price faster and stops low-AMH or high-BMI patients reading PURE prices that don't apply to them. Fewer surprises at consultation, fewer wasted appointments.
at: CARE (BMI calculator, NHS calculator); Bourn Hall (fertility self-assessment)

title: Fix the conflicting PURE criteria
seen: Two different sets of PURE criteria are live today (prices page and PURE page).
idea: Agree the current criteria with the clinical lead and make both pages match this week, before any build work.
payback: Costs an hour. Prevents a patient booking against the wrong criteria and a complaint later.

title: Show the HFEA rating next to every add-on
seen: EmbryoScope, EmbryoGlue, PICSI, endometrial receptivity testing (£1,308–£1,623) and DNA fragmentation (£462) are sold without the HFEA's evidence ratings. HFEA rates time-lapse and PICSI black (no effect on the chance of a baby), EmbryoGlue amber and endometrial receptivity testing red. The EmbryoScope page says it "can improve your IVF treatment".
idea: A short 'Add-ons and the evidence' panel on the prices and package pages: the HFEA colour, what it means, why the clinic still includes it (EmbryoScope and EmbryoGlue are bundled at no extra cost), and when it's genuinely indicated.
payback: Candidly, this could trim some optional add-on sales (ERA, PICSI). But it's what an NHS clinic should be known for, it protects against complaints and press risk, and it gives the clinic a trust advantage private rivals find hard to copy. Trust converts.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' ("no unnecessary add-ons")

title: Ways to pay page
seen: Staged payments for Duo and Multi are a real advantage but appear only in the prices intro. No finance option is mentioned.
idea: A 'Ways to pay' page: staged payments, what's due when, cancellation refunds, and (if the Trust agrees) a regulated finance partner or interest-free instalments.
payback: Affordability is the main reason self-funders delay or go elsewhere. Every major private rival offers finance. Even without a partner, explaining staged payments clearly makes £11,540 feel like £8,390 now and £1,575 later.
at: Bourn Hall (finance, refund programme); CARE (Carepay); Hewitt (financial packages)

title: Lead with staged payments on package pages
seen: Duo and Multi-Cycle payments are only paid for the cycles you go ahead with, but this is buried.
idea: Put 'Pay for cycle 1 now, later cycles only if you need them' at the top of each Duo and Multi page, with the three amounts.
payback: Nudges people towards the higher-value packages with no build cost.

title: Secure online enquiry and self-referral
seen: There is no enquiry or referral form anywhere on the site. Self-referral is "by email or post". Out of hours, the only option is an email address.
idea: A short, secure enquiry form (name, contact, how you'd like to be funded, what you're interested in, best time to call) and a fuller self-referral form with uploads for previous results. Confirmation page with what happens next and how long it takes.
payback: The biggest single lever. Every competitor checked captures enquiries on the page. A form works at 10pm when people are researching, lets the team prioritise call-backs, and for the first time lets the clinic count leads and see which pages produce them.
at: Bourn Hall (embedded CRM form); Herts & Essex (consultation form); Guy's and St Thomas' (on-page enquiry form)

title: Book a call or consultation online
seen: Appointments are booked by phone (01223 349010, options 2–4) or email.
idea: Let people pick a slot for a free 15-minute call with the patient team, and later book a paid initial consultation (£220) or fertility assessment (£375–£595) with a deposit.
payback: Booked calls convert far better than unanswered emails, and paid self-booking turns interest into revenue without staff time. Bourn Hall, the nearest rival, makes 'Book a discovery call' its main button.
at: Bourn Hall (discovery call); Herts & Essex (book consultation)

title: Information sessions people can see and book on the page
seen: Free information sessions run on Tuesday evenings by phone, booked through a TryBooking link that opens a new site. The homepage doesn't say when the next one is.
idea: Show the next three dates on the homepage and key service pages, embed the booking, and add an occasional in-person open evening at Kefford House or a recorded webinar for those who prefer to listen first.
payback: An attended session is the warmest lead the clinic gets. Bourn Hall runs a Cambridge open evening a few miles away, and Herts & Essex puts its next open evening date on the homepage. Showing a date creates a reason to act now.
at: Herts & Essex (next open evening on the homepage); Bourn Hall (Cambridge open evening); CARE (online events)

title: Sticky 'Start your journey' bar on mobile
seen: On a phone, the only actions are buried in page copy; the prices page has none above the fold.
idea: A slim bar with Call, Book an information session and Enquire, on service, price and package pages.
payback: Cheap to add and keeps the next step one tap away on long pages, which is where people make up their minds.

title: Measure what the site produces
seen: GA4 and Google Tag Manager are already installed, but there are no forms to measure and no sign of event tracking on phone, email, TryBooking or price-list clicks.
idea: Set up GA4 events for tel: and mailto: taps, TryBooking clicks, price-list downloads and (later) form submissions, and a simple monthly report: visits, leads, sessions booked, by page.
payback: Doesn't earn anything by itself, but it's how you prove the rest of this list pays back. Without it, nobody can say which change made a difference.

title: 'Send me the guide' email sign-up
seen: Nothing captures the many visitors who aren't ready to call yet.
idea: Offer a plain guide (costs, steps, questions to ask any clinic) in exchange for an email address, followed by a few useful emails and the next information session date.
payback: Most fertility research happens weeks or months before booking. Keeping in touch is how the clinic is still in the frame when they're ready.

title: 'Who are you?' entry points
seen: The hero names heterosexual couples, same sex couples, single women, single men and transgender people, but the navigation is organised by service (Assessment, Treatments, Preservation, Donor).
idea: A row of entry points under the hero and in the menu: couples, female couples, single women, single men, trans and non-binary people, planning ahead (egg freezing), NHS-referred, started elsewhere. Each lands on a page that explains their likely route, price and next step.
payback: Female couples, single women and egg-freezers are almost all self-funded, so they're the most valuable visitors. Every competitor checked speaks to them by name in the menu; Cambridge IVF only does it in one paragraph.
at: Bourn Hall, CARE, Herts & Essex (audience menus); Hewitt ("How can we help you?")

title: Your journey, step by step
seen: The 'Your journey' section page returns a 404, and the treatment steps are spread across the lab page, the support page and package pages.
idea: A single timeline: enquiry, information session, assessment, consultation, treatment cycle, test, early pregnancy and the Rosie. Each step says how long it takes, what it costs and who you'll see.
payback: Reduces 'what happens next' calls and makes the clinic's NHS advantage (care right through to the Rosie) visible.

title: Fix the two broken menu links
seen: /your-journey/ and /your-journey/coronavirus-and-pregancy/ ('Early pregnancy and Coronavirus') return 'Page not found' from the main menu.
idea: Remove the coronavirus item and either publish a Your journey landing page or point the menu at an existing page.
payback: Ten minutes. Broken links in the main menu undermine a clinic asking people for £5,000+.

title: Fix the inner-page theme
seen: Inner pages carry the body class 'theme-- -ivf', so the IVF theme never applies and every hero is NHS blue instead of IVF pink.
idea: Correct the theme setting on inner page templates so they use the IVF accent bar and colours already in the stylesheet.
payback: A small developer fix that makes the site look like one brand rather than two.

title: Use the empty right-hand column
seen: At desktop, content pages sit in a 640px column with nothing to the right.
idea: Use the space for a sticky 'Next step' panel (price, next information session, enquire) on service and package pages.
payback: Puts the call to action beside the decision-making content at no content cost.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (in-page links and form)

title: Search results page title
seen: The search results page title is blank ('| Cambridge IVF') and searching 'price' lists Terms and conditions before Prices.
idea: Add a title and promote key pages (prices, information sessions, egg freezing) for common terms.
payback: Small, but search users are usually looking for a price or a phone number.

title: Current success rates, by age, in plain HTML
seen: The success rates page uses 2019–2020 data ("correct as of 8th January 2024"), shown as PNG images. The HFEA now publishes 2024 data for the clinic: 31% births per embryo transferred against 35% nationally, 'consistent with national average'.
idea: Rebuild the page with the latest HFEA figures as accessible charts, add births per egg collection (cumulative) by age, and explain honestly what the numbers do and don't tell you. Link to the HFEA profile.
payback: Success rates is in the main menu and is one of the first pages comparison shoppers read. Five-year-old data reads as something to hide. Being upfront, with the HFEA's own framing, is safer and more persuasive.
at: Bourn Hall (success by age, 2025 outcomes); CARE (Univfy personalised prediction)

title: One heritage date
seen: "Experience dates back to 1992" (success rates), "1994" (PURE page) and "set up in 2011, builds on 20 years" (health professionals). The HFEA says licensed since 1992.
idea: Use one line everywhere, e.g. 'Licensed by the HFEA since 1992; in Kefford House since 2011'.
payback: Ten minutes; consistency is a trust signal.

title: Refresh patient stories
seen: Five stories, the oldest from 2013, mostly heterosexual couples. Nothing from egg freezers, female couples or single women.
idea: Collect six new stories (with consent) that match the entry points in idea 15, with a photo or short video where people are willing, and link each from its matching page.
payback: People buy from people like them. Stories placed on the right page do more than a stories index.

title: Lift the HFEA patient rating
seen: HFEA patient rating 2 out of 5 from only 22 ratings, shown on every HFEA clinic search and comparison. Inspection rating is 5 out of 5.
idea: Ask every patient at the review appointment to rate the clinic on the HFEA site (a card, a QR code and a follow-up email), and act on what the low scores say about costs.
payback: With 22 ratings, a few dozen more will move the score. The HFEA comparison is where many self-funders shortlist clinics, so this may be the cheapest revenue lever on the list.

title: Meet the team
seen: No staff profiles beyond a video of the service lead on the homepage.
idea: Short profiles for consultants, embryologists, nurses, counsellors and the patient team, with photos, special interests and the information session they run.
payback: Faces lower the barrier to that first call, and consultants' names are what people search once they've heard of them.
at: Hewitt (Our People); Herts & Essex, Bourn Hall (Meet the team)

title: Say plainly why an NHS clinic
seen: The NHS and CUH advantages (Rosie maternity hospital, genetics, counselling within two weeks, income reinvested in CUH women's and children's services) are scattered across five pages.
idea: A 'Why an NHS clinic?' section on the homepage and why-choose page, with four concrete proof points.
payback: It's the one thing private rivals can't claim. Making it obvious justifies the price and the choice.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (consultant-led NHS specialist care)

title: Show the building
seen: The facilities page lists rooms and equipment in text only.
idea: A photo gallery or short walkthrough of Kefford House: reception, consultation rooms, recovery, the lab.
payback: Reassures nervous first-timers. Nice to have rather than a revenue driver.

title: Update the NHS funding page
seen: "Cambridge and Peterborough CCG have recently announced that they are to re-introduce NHS funded IVF – further details... to be added here as soon as they are available." CCGs were replaced by integrated care boards in July 2022. The health professionals page also refers to 'CCG criteria'.
idea: Replace with current ICB criteria (or links to each ICB's policy), a 'Am I likely to be eligible for NHS funding?' summary, and a clear route for people who aren't (self-funding from £2,900).
payback: People who find they're not NHS-eligible are the clinic's next self-funded patients, if the page catches them with a clear alternative.
at: CARE (NHS calculator); Hewitt (NHS funding and criteria)

title: Retire the 'Postcode lottery' copy
seen: Refers to "36 of 209 CCG's", "Jane Ellison, the Minister for Public Health" and a closed e-petition.
idea: Remove it or replace with a short, current explanation of NHS funding with links to Fertility Network UK.
payback: Ten minutes. Dated politics on a clinical site makes everything else look dated too.

title: Clean up legacy links
seen: Links to the old domain cambridge-ivf.org.uk on the egg freezing and health professionals pages, and Outlook 'safelinks' wrappers containing a staff email address on the feedback page.
idea: Replace with direct links and add a broken-link check to the monthly routine.
payback: Hygiene and a small privacy fix.

title: Stop labelling information as 'Non-urgent advice'
seen: The support information page (about 41,000 characters) uses the NHS 'Non-urgent advice' card for everything, and repeats the whole lab page.
idea: Use plain headings and accordions, and link to the lab page rather than duplicating it.
payback: Clearer reading; NHS care cards mean something specific to NHS users.

title: Tidy the prices page
seen: Typos ("chalmydia", "IICSI", "Human and Fertilisation (HFEA)", "pregnancy scan.pregnancy scan."), the add-on list repeated under nearly every package, and overseas transport with a special export directive (£300) priced below without (£330).
idea: Correct the copy, show add-ons once in their own table, and check the transport fees.
payback: Typos on a price list make people wonder what else is wrong. An hour of editing.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (itemised price lists)

title: Remove 'under development' notices
seen: The services and patient information leaflets pages both say "this page is currently under development".
idea: Finish or remove the note; group leaflets by stage of treatment.
payback: Quick confidence fix.

title: Keep the egg bank page on topic
seen: The donor egg page includes advice on improving semen quality and names a supplement brand.
idea: Move the semen advice to an andrology page and drop the brand mention.
payback: An NHS page naming a commercial supplement is a small reputational risk.

title: Refresh the pregnancy care page
seen: Leads on the Rosie's 2013 royal opening.
idea: Lead instead on what joined-up care means for a Cambridge IVF patient: early pregnancy scan, handover to the Rosie, specialist services.
payback: Turns a dated page into a selling point.

title: Egg freezing hub
seen: The egg freezing page is about 750 characters, with no price, no success-by-age information and no FAQs. It links to the HFEA and the prices page on the old domain.
idea: A proper hub for people planning ahead: who it's for, what happens, price and storage costs, success by age at freezing, FAQs, upcoming information sessions, stories, and a 'Book an egg freezing consultation' button.
payback: Egg freezers are self-funded, research for months, and pay £3,675 to £7,875 up front plus £346 a year storage for years after. It's one of the fastest-growing parts of the market and the current page barely competes for it.
at: Bourn Hall, CARE (dedicated egg freezing sections)

title: Book and pay for private semen analysis online
seen: The andrology service does 500+ analyses a month across three labs, with 26–34 working-day waits. Private tests (£189, DNA fragmentation £462) are booked by phone.
idea: Online booking with payment for private semen analysis, with the current wait time shown at the point of booking.
payback: Takes calls off a busy line and turns 'I'll ring tomorrow' into a paid booking. Some of these men and their partners are tomorrow's IVF patients.
at: Bourn Hall (semen analysis); Hewitt (self-funded semen analysis)

title: Online pre-screen for donors
seen: The sperm donor questionnaire is a PDF. Donor sperm and eggs are in short supply; the clinic offers donors a free PURE IVF cycle.
idea: A short online eligibility pre-screen for potential sperm donors, leading to a call back.
payback: Every recruited donor supports several treatment cycles (and the clinic's donor cycles are £6,990 to £7,990). Removing the print-and-post step increases the number who start.

title: Pay storage fees online
seen: Annual storage costs £346 a year for eggs, embryos or sperm. We couldn't see any way to pay it, or other fees, online.
idea: An online payment page for storage renewals and admin fees, using GOV.UK Pay or the Trust's existing payment provider.
payback: Faster cash collection and less chasing. Storage is recurring income, so smoothing it pays back every year.
at: Guy's and St Thomas' (GOV.UK Pay payment portal)

title: Modern referral forms for GPs and consultants
seen: The semen cryopreservation referral is a .doc, and the referral pages refer to CCG criteria.
idea: Update the forms and criteria, and offer an online referral where the Trust's systems allow.
payback: Referrers are a steady source of NHS and self-funded patients. Making referral easy keeps them sending.

title: Switching clinics made simple
seen: The 'Started treatment elsewhere?' page is a few sentences with a 'click here' link.
idea: Explain moving embryos or eggs to Cambridge IVF, what records to bring, the transport fee, and a dedicated enquiry route.
payback: Patients unhappy elsewhere are already self-funding and ready to start. A clear switch route wins them with copy alone.
at: Herts & Essex (support for people treated overseas)

title: Search visibility basics
seen: Several pages share the same meta description; search result titles and descriptions don't mention price or 'NHS' consistently.
idea: Unique titles and descriptions for the top 20 pages, FAQ sections on key pages, and a check of how the clinic appears for 'IVF Cambridge', 'egg freezing Cambridge' and 'IVF cost Cambridge'.
payback: Bourn Hall competes for the same local searches. Better listings bring more of those searchers to Cambridge IVF for free.

title: Accessible charts and links
seen: Success-rate charts are images; many links read "(opens in a new tab) (opens in a new tab)". The accessibility statement lists known gaps.
idea: Replace chart images with HTML tables or accessible charts and fix duplicated link labels.
payback: A legal duty for an NHS site, and screen-reader users are patients too.
